## Passages to take up

Your open passages, from your journal handoff (notes/journal.md), quoted as you wrote them:

> Open passages: none

The critic's notes from its last visit (notes/critic.md), quoted as the critic wrote them. You decide what to take from them.

> From the critic's visit at the end of a sitting:
>
> Yes, the birches now sit in the canopy's shade. In the full view and in squint they dim as they go up into the leaves and are brightest where they stand clear against the haze, so the falls have the white to themselves again. The rust lobes biting into their shadow edges did the rest: in the edges view the trunks' outlines inside the canopy are broken and dim instead of running unbroken top to bottom.
>
> What the picture does well, it now does throughout. In squint, the light is one vertical chain: glow, then brink, then curtain, then foam, then the gold column in the pool. The dark banks frame it, with light only on their crests, which commits the picture to backlight. The hardest edges and the strongest value contrast are on the falls and nowhere else. The things you fought over the longest now read as what they are at full view: the frayed sides of the curtain, the foam lying broken on the water, the rocks seated at a level waterline, the left loaf running off the edge as the toe of the bank.
>
> I looked for a change that matters and didn't find one I'd make. The one thing I noticed is the two orange leaf collars where the canopy crosses the trunks. They sit at almost the same height, so they read a little alike. But your own reflections lesson applies here: a small, quiet error on a dry passage is cheaper to accept than to fix.
>
> The painting is finished. In the next sitting, don't make any marks. End it by looking at the whole canvas and one detail crop in normal color, then sign off.

You're back at the easel. The painting is as you left it. Your brief is in BRIEF.md and your journal in notes/journal.md. Read your journal handoff and apply its practical lessons before acting. Take up your open passages: look at each in an appropriate detail crop in normal color, then improve it or accept it as it is, and say which in your journal, with your reason. A passage you've resolved or accepted comes off the list. You may finish with imperfections you deliberately accept. A fresh look at the whole canvas and detail crops in normal color can show passages the list doesn't have yet; add them to it. Continue one campaign at a time, inspecting the whole picture and relevant detail before writing the next campaign's code. Let the result inform your next action and check local repairs against the whole picture; reconsider the composition or method if a repair repeats the problem. Judge unfamiliar mixtures and marks through small laid trials on the intended substrate after the intended treatment. Carry forward the observed material conditions and treat broader rules as hypotheses. Before retrying a failed recipe, identify what has changed and why that could address the observed failure. Record what you observed and what remains uncertain. You can keep working for hours if you like, and the painting's simulated time is yours to use, whether that means days or years. Enjoy it. At the end of the sitting, record an updated handoff in your journal and last reply: the `Open passages:` list as it now stands (`Open passages: none` when nothing is open) and the practical lessons that still apply. The painting is finished when you end a sitting in which you made no marks on the painting and looked at the whole canvas and at a detail crop in normal color, even if the list still names passages. Record your reflections in your journal before you end that sitting.

Your previous sitting's reply:
I painted on it again this sitting, so it isn't formally finished yet. No passages are open, and next sitting should be a look-only check.

**Where the Light Comes Down (Autumn Falls)** is a tall autumn woodland lit from behind. A gold glow in the trees, under an arch of rust and amber leaves, lights a small four-strand waterfall over dark wet rock. Two white birches stand on the right bank, and the still pool below holds a grayed gold reflection of the glow.

**What changed this sitting:** I worked on the two birches, following the critic's notes.
- **Dimmed tops.** Inside the canopy the birches were nearly as light as the falls and competed with them for the eye. Four thin, staggered glaze layers on each trunk now darken them upward into the canopy's shade. A thin lit edge stays on the side facing the glow.
- **Edges and overlap.** Even dimmed, the trunks lay on the canopy like strips of tape. Small soft lobes of the canopy's own rust now bite into each trunk's shadow-side edge, and one leaf mass crosses each trunk where the canopy ends. The birches now pass behind the lowest leaves and come out lit into the haze. The falls are again the brightest thing in the picture.

**Tried and wiped off: the birch reflections.** The critic pointed out that they start right under the right-hand rock, though the birches stand behind the bushes, so their reflections should start lower. I tried five ways of covering the tops of the pale streaks on the painting itself, and two more on the scratch canvas. Every cover made a shape louder than the error: gray curtains, icicle shapes, blotches, a ladder of dark dashes. I wiped them all off and kept the reflections as they are. At full view they read as the trunks' reflections, and they are quieter than the central gold column.

Open passages: none

**Practical lessons that still apply:**
- **Lifting:** wet paint over dry lifts cleanly with a rag dipped in solvent, so trying something on the painting itself is cheap. Judge it while it's still wet.
- **Glazing the birches:** for the umber/smalt glaze over dry birch white, medium .75 gives a clean film. At .6 it mottles, and at .8–.9 it vanishes. To grade it without visible rings, use 3–4 nested layers with ragged, slanted bottoms, clipped to the trunk.
- **Losing an edge into foliage:** use soft, lobed shapes along the measured edge, painted with short strokes in the neighbour's measured mix. Plain tapered shapes painted flat make crisp stripes.
- **Covering lights:** a glaze can dim a light but can't remove it. An opaque cover over a soft, blended light on dry paint always gets an edge of its own.
- **Measured mixes, dry values (0–255 scale):**
  - deeprust .55 / leafrust .25 / orangeleaf .1 / amber .1 ≈ 111, for the rust canopy.
  - deeprust .85 / leafrust .15 ≈ 99, for the darker canopy.
  - waterdark .85 / deeprust .11 / haze .02 / amber .02 ≈ 71, for the pool under the banks.
- **Palette:** it holds 16 piles. To free slots, scrape the piles made most recently.

**Reflection:** a value step alone didn't put the birches in the space. The overlap and the softened edges did. With the reflections, an error that is soft and already dry turned out to be cheaper to accept than to fix.

## BRIEF.md

# Paint a picture

Compose and paint one original picture in the technique of wet-on-wet
painting, at the easel, a simulator of oil paint on linen. The place,
subject and composition are yours to invent. Work from knowledge and the
notes in your studio; don't use reference images or image models.

## Your studio
- The folder [local path redacted] this brief, your notes and the easel.
- The easel's tools are `paint`, `look`, `note`, `status` and `log`;
  notes/easel_guide.md explains them.
- There is no undo. To change a passage, paint over it, or lift wet
  paint with a rag or a brush.
- You mix your own paint on the palette, from the tubes, in the
  proportions you choose.
- Time passes on the painting's own clock: every mark takes the time a
  hand takes, and `wait(minutes)` lets it rest, as long as you like; paint
  dries as that time passes. Real time between chunks doesn't count.

## The rules of the studio
- Paint shapes and marks, not computed pictures: don't encode an image in
  masks, amounts or proportions.
- Shapes are drawn, not copied: don't make a mask or stroke by mirroring
  or rotating another mask's or stroke's coordinates. A shape that mirrors
  another is drawn as its own shape, not as `m:at(x, 2*H - y)` or
  `m:at(W - x, y)`. Moving a shape and reusing your own helpers are fine.

## What to read
notes/easel_guide.md; notes/techniques.md; notes/studio_notes.md;
notes/research/wet_on_wet.md (the technique's materials and method) and
notes/research/oil_paint_physics.md as needed. The wet-on-wet note
describes real materials; the tubes in your box are the ones listed in
notes/easel_guide.md, and you mix your colors from them. The note's
closing section proposes how a simulator might work, but
notes/easel_guide.md describes what this easel does: the ground is dry
when painting starts, and any wet film is paint you lay over it.

After choosing a subject or technical question, use `reference` to search
the studio's reference library, or `reference_list` to browse its titles.
Read a result with `reference` by its id; follow next_page
until it is null to read the full text.

Another painter visits your studio as a critic, at the end of each sitting
and whenever you ask for a visit with `ask_critic`. The critic looks at the
painting with the same `look` you use and reads your journal and the note
you give `ask_critic` (kept in notes/to_critic.md); it doesn't paint. It
writes what it would fix and why in notes/critic.md, which you get at the
start of your next sitting or as `ask_critic`'s reply.

## Choosing the picture
Before you paint, write eight different pictures you could make from this brief in notes/concepts.md, numbered 1 to 8, each in a sentence or two. After each one, write your estimate of how many painters out of a hundred given this brief would make that picture. The studio sets aside the two with the highest estimates, rolls a die among the other six and tells you which one is yours. You make every decision from there, and the picture can develop wherever the painting takes it.

## Working
Work one campaign at a time. After laying a campaign, inspect the whole picture in normal color and relevant detail before writing the code for the next campaign. Let what you see inform the next action; record what changes or why continuing unchanged serves the picture.

After the first large masses, consider whether the whole picture produces your intended effect: how its large shapes, values and spatial relationships support it, and whether anything weakens it. Improve a weakening relationship in the large masses, or deliberately accept it with your reason, before you build detail over them. After a local repair, check its effect on the whole picture. If the repair recreates the problem, reconsider the composition or method before expanding it.

Before repeating an unfamiliar mixture or stroke, inspect a small trial, on the scratch canvas beside the painting (`scratch: true`) or on the painting, laid on the intended substrate after the intended treatment, alongside the existing marks in a detail crop. A held pile shows thick paint on steel; use the laid trial to judge its effect on the picture. For material trials and repairs, keep useful observations in your journal: substrate and wetness, recipe ratios, medium or thinner, brush load, coverage and the viewed result. Carry forward the conditions that mattered and label broader rules as hypotheses until a further trial isolates them.

- You make every artistic decision.
- Keep exploring what interests you. You’re free to reconsider a passage,
  change approach and discover where the painting can go.
- Keep a working journal with `note` as you go: your own working notes.
  You can revise them.
- You may sign the painting.
- Take your time and enjoy painting. You can keep working for hours,
  exploring and revisiting passages.
- An oil painting can develop over simulated years. Whether yours takes
  one simulated day or a thousand, that time is yours to use.
- Your journal handoff at the end of each sitting lists the passages
  still open under a line reading `Open passages:`, or reads
  `Open passages: none` when nothing is open, and the next sitting opens
  with that list. The painting is finished when you end a sitting in
  which you made no marks on the painting and looked at the whole canvas
  and at a detail crop in normal color, even if the list still names
  passages. Record your reflections in your journal before you end that
  sitting.

## Your reply
When you stop working, reply with the painting's title if you give it one
and a few sentences about the picture.

## Your journal (notes/journal.md)

Your own notes, quoted as you wrote them:

> - day 1, 09:00: ## Sitting 1 — plan
>   Concept 4: autumn woodland stream falling over mossy rocks, small waterfall, white birches, gold/rust foliage reflected in pool.
>   Canvas: 480 mm wide, aspect 0.8 (W 1000, H 1250), linen 18x15, ground lead white 10 + yellow ochre 0.4 + raw umber 0.15, 120 µm knife, texture 0.25 (warm cream).
>   Composition (portrait): glow in the back woods upper left-center (~x380,y300), canopy gold/rust across the top with sky gaps; ledge ~y585 across middle; falls x~400–560 dropping to ~y780 in two strands split by a rock; pool y 780–1250 with vertical reflections of canopy and birches, foam at base; two birches on right bank (x~760, ~870), a slimmer one left behind the rocks; mossy rock lower left foreground, floating leaves.
>   Values: lights = falls, foam, birches, glow; darks = rock under the lip, pool depths near banks, deep woods at edges; mids = foliage, moss.
>   Method (wet-on-wet): a thin oily wet film first, then back to front, dark before light, all into open paint within the day: glow/back woods → canopy masses → rocks/ledge (knife) → pool base + vertical reflection pulls + horizontal passes → falls pulled down + foam → birches (thick light over wet dark) → moss lights, leaves, twigs, highlights.
>   Palette: lead white; gold = chrome yellow + ochre (+white); rust = red earth + ochre + touch vermilion; darks = Prussian + red earth + umber; moss = green earth + chrome + ochre, Prussian + chrome + ochre; water = white + cobalt; birch shadow = white + smalt + umber.
> - day 1, 09:00: Scratch trials 1 (dry cream ground, all into open paint, day 1 morning):

## Sitting 7 (day 645) — look-only check, no marks. The painting is finished.

Looked at the whole canvas in normal color, then at one detail crop of the falls, foam and pool head (x 300–720, y 600–1020, 2.4×). I made no marks.
- Whole view: the light runs in one vertical chain: glow under the canopy arch, then the brink, the four-strand curtain, the foam, and the grayed gold column in the pool. The dark banks frame it, with light only on their crests. The birches dim into the canopy's shade and are brightest against the haze, below the leaves. The mid-ground rocks sit on a level waterline. The foreground rock anchors the lower left.
- Detail: up close, the lower curtain shows the separate streaks of its strokes, the foam's trails are lacy and the caps under the brink are a little boxy. All of these were accepted in earlier sittings as close-up faults that read correctly at full view, and they still do. Nothing new showed. The critic noticed the two orange leaf collars where the canopy crosses the birches, at nearly the same height. I'm accepting them as they are: a small, quiet rhyme on dry paint.

Open passages: none

Practical lessons that still apply (for any later work on this canvas or the next):
- Wet paint over DRY lifts clean with a dipped rag (dip 1.0, pressure 1.0, width 12–24, 2–3 passes each way, fresh rags), so trials on the painting itself are cheap. Judge a mark while it is still open.
- Clip any pass that has a hard boundary. Print mask:area() and look with mask= before painting. Use low-frequency noise for ragged edges.
- Glazes: umber/smalt at medium .75 over dry white gives a clean film. Grade with nested films that have noisy, slanted bottoms. A glaze dims a light but cannot remove it. An opaque cover over a soft, blended light on dry paint always gets an edge of its own.
- Boundaries carry the reading. Break them with the neighbour's own paint, in tapered, unequal shapes (wedges, lobes, ribbons).
- Measure a mix on scratch and let it dry before using it as a cover. Judge trials on the real substrate, with its texture and its neighbours.

Reflection: this painting took about 645 days of easel time across seven sittings. Most of that went into one lesson, learned again in passage after passage: a shape reads as false while its boundary is one even line, and it comes alive when the neighbouring paint breaks that line. The brink, the curtain's sides, the foam's bottom, the waterline under the rocks and the birches' edges in the canopy all worked this way. The second lesson was when to stop. The reflections, the lenticels, the loaves, the mist and the orange smear each got louder with repair, and accepting them was the better painting. The wet-on-wet plan from day 1 (background, then masses, then falls, then lights, all into open paint) carried the big structure: the glowing back woods and the misty ghost trunks still come from the first day. The falls, though, had to be rebuilt later over dry paint, strand by strand. Title: "Where the Light Comes Down (Autumn Falls)".

**Where the Light Comes Down (Autumn Falls)** is finished. This sitting I only looked: first at the whole canvas, then at a close crop of the falls, foam and the head of the pool, both in normal color. I made no marks, and nothing new showed.

It's a tall autumn woodland lit from behind. A gold glow sits deep in the trees, under an arch of rust and amber leaves. That light comes down through one vertical chain: the thin stream at the brink, a four-strand waterfall that frays and widens as it drops between dark wet rocks, foam that breaks up and drifts on the water, and a grayed gold column in the still pool. The banks stay dark, with light only along their crests. Two white birches dim as they rise into the canopy's shade and are brightest where they stand clear against the haze.

Up close, the lower curtain shows the separate streaks of its strokes, the foam is a little lacy and the caps under the brink are slightly boxy. I accepted these in earlier sittings because they read correctly at full view, and they still do. I'm also leaving the two leaf collars on the birches, which sit at almost the same height. It's a small rhyme on dry paint, and fixing it would cost more than it's worth.

Open passages: none

**Practical lessons that still apply:**
- **Lifting:** wet paint over dry lifts cleanly with rags dipped in solvent, so trying something on the painting itself is cheap. Judge it while it's still wet.
- **Hard boundaries:** confine any pass that has a hard boundary (a waterline, the brink, the edge of the curtain) to that boundary. Check a mask's area and shape before painting through it, and use slowly varying noise for ragged edges.
- **Glazes:**
  - Raw umber and smalt with medium .75 gives a clean film over dry white.
  - To grade a glaze, lay several nested layers whose bottom edges are ragged and slanted.
  - A glaze can dim a light but can't remove it, and an opaque cover over a soft, blended light always gets an edge of its own.
- **Boundaries:** edges carry the reading. Break an even line with the neighbouring passage's own paint, in tapered, unequal shapes.
- **Trials:** mix a color, let it dry on the scratch canvas and measure it before using it to cover something. Judge every trial on the real surface, with its texture and its neighbours.

**Reflection:** most of this painting taught one lesson, over and over. A shape looks false while its boundary is one even line, and it comes alive when the paint next to it breaks that line. That happened at the brink, the sides of the curtain, the bottom of the foam, the waterline under the rocks and the birches' edges in the canopy. The second lesson was when to stop: some passages only got louder when I repaired them, and accepting them made the better painting.
